title: Bonku Babu’s Friend
tagline: A timid teacher, twenty-two years of ridicule, and one night a spaceship lands in the bamboo grove.

overview.intro: The first prescribed story of Class IX is a science-fiction comedy of manners. Bonkubihari Dutta — Bonku Babu — has taught geography and Bengali in the village of Kankurgachhi for twenty-two years, and for twenty-two years he has been the village’s good-natured amusement: cartoons on the blackboard, glue on the chair, a rocket lit behind him at Kali Puja. He swallows it all because he fears losing the job. At the Saturday evening gatherings at Sripati Majumdar’s house the mockery sharpens, and when Bonku gently suggests that visitors from another planet might one day land here, Bhairav Chakravarthy and the others assure him that no sensible creature would choose Kankurgachhi. Then a light Bonku spotted is claimed by Nidhi Babu, and a real visitor — Ang, from the planet Craneus — lands anyway. This chapter follows the story’s arc: humiliation, encounter, transformation, and the new Bonku who faces his tormentors without flinching. The themes are Ray’s usual kindness — that courage is not given to the loud, and that a person changes when someone treats him as an equal.

learn.title: Before you read: Ray’s gentle science fiction

blocks.text: Satyajit Ray is known to most Class IX readers as the filmmaker behind the Apu trilogy, but he was also a writer of stories and essays, and “Bonku Babu’s Friend” (originally “Bonkubabur Bondhu”) belongs to his lighter, speculative work. Published summaries place it in the tradition of comic science fiction: an ordinary, decent man meets the extraordinary, and the extraordinary behaves better than the people at home. Read it, first, as a comedy — the humour lives in the village conversations and in the confident wrongness of men who insist that visitors from space would have better taste than Kankurgachhi. Read it, second, as a story about dignity: every laugh the village enjoys at Bonku’s expense costs him something small, and the story measures those costs so that the reader feels the size of what happens when he finally stops paying them. As you read, note how Ray gives Bonku a rich inner life — his storytelling, his patience, his quiet arithmetic of fear — while the loud men around him are drawn almost entirely from the outside.

items: Genre: comic science fiction with a social heart.
Ray writes the ridiculed man from within and the ridiculers from without.
The humour never excuses the cruelty; the story keeps both in view.
Watch the titles and names — Babu, the respectful suffix — used as instruments of mockery.

learn.title: The story in outline: from mockery to the encounter

blocks.text: Published summaries describe the story’s movement in four stages. First, establishment: Bonku Babu teaches in Kankurgachhi, and no one has ever seen him angry; his students invent new ways to humiliate him each year, and he endures them because he believes he would find no other post. Second, the gatherings: at Sripati Majumdar’s house the regulars — among them Nidhi Babu, Chandi Babu, Ramkanai and Bhairav Chakravarthy — trade opinions about ghosts, satellites and rockets, and Bonku is kept chiefly for amusement. When he says he is not afraid of ghosts, they arrange the prank under the tamarind tree that injures his neck and ruins his new kurta. When he speaks of a light he has seen in the sky, Nidhi Babu claims the sighting as his own, and Bonku says nothing. Third, the provocation: the talk turns to space travel, and Bonku’s gentle question — what if they came here? — is met with the assurance that no visitor from another planet would waste itself on Kankurgachhi. Fourth, the visit itself: on a night shortly afterwards a glowing object comes down in the bamboo grove, and Ang steps out of it. The summaries agree that Ang befriends Bonku, treats him as an equal, shows him wonders, and later lifts him above the very village that mocked him — and that the story closes with a changed Bonku confronting the gathered men, who cannot recognise the confidence in him.

blocks.text: Bonku Babu is the story’s centre and its lesson: gentle, patient, a gifted storyteller whose African and polar tales enchant the few children who like him, and whose fear of losing his post keeps him silent through twenty-two years of insult. He is not a fool — he asks the exact right question about visitors from space — he is merely without an ally. Ang, the visitor from Craneus, is the ally: courteous, curious and completely uninterested in status, he speaks to Bonku as an equal, and published study guides read his behaviour as the standard the village fails to meet. The men of the gatherings form a chorus of small cruelty. Bhairav Chakravarthy slaps Bonku’s back hard and calls him Bumkum; Sripati Majumdar, important enough to be certain about everything, pronounces that aliens have better places to go; Nidhi Babu takes Bonku’s sighting for himself. Read together they are a study in how a group distributes a single victim among it. The students deserve a separate note: each year a new batch arrives and inherits the tradition — cruelty, the story suggests, is taught by letting it continue unchallenged.

items.text: Bonku endures the rocket prank at Kali Puja because he believes no other post awaits him.
items.note: Security, not weakness, is the reason for his silence.

items.text: Nidhi Babu claims the sighting of the light that Bonku had shown him.
items.note: Theft of credit is the last preparation for the night visit.

learn.title: The night encounter and what it changes

blocks.text: The encounter is brief in outline and enormous in effect. A glowing object descends into the bamboo grove; from it comes Ang, an alien whose technology and knowledge exceed anything the village argued about on Saturday evenings. What matters more than the wonders is the manner: Ang is interested, polite and friendly — he addresses Bonku by name and as a companion, the first creature in the story to do so. Published summaries stress two effects. Internally, Bonku’s fear unwinds: being treated as an equal by a superior being reveals that his lowly place was assigned, not earned, by the village. Externally, the story grants him a change the neighbours can see — the later gathering meets a Bonku who answers back, who refers to what he knows and what he has seen, and who leaves the men astonished at his confidence. The science fiction, in other words, is a device: Ray needs something larger than Kankurgachhi to show Bonku that Kankurgachhi’s opinion is small. The comedy survives to the end — the men’s faces when their certainties fail are funny — but the tenderness is the point.

items: Ang lands in the bamboo grove and treats Bonku as an equal.
The wonders shown are less important than the courtesy shown.
The internal change: fear unwinds when status is removed.
The external change: the gathered men meet a Bonku who answers back.
Ray uses the extraterrestrial to measure how small the village’s scale was.

learn.title: Themes: courage, self-discovery and the cost of ridicule

blocks.text: The story carries three themes that examination answers should keep apart. Self-discovery: Bonku does not become brave by an act of will; he discovers he was always capable, once someone removes the lie that told him otherwise — the alien’s friendship functions as a mirror in which he sees himself. Courage: the story relocates courage from loudness to endurance and then to speech — Bonku bears twenty-two years (endurance), faces the ghost-prank without collapsing (nerve), and finally speaks without flinching (speech). The ridicule of the weak: Ray examines how communities manufacture a target — through pranks, stolen credit, derisive nicknames and the annual inheritance of the custom by new students — and shows that the target’s gentleness is not consent. A fourth, quieter theme is knowledge itself: the men dismiss satellites, rockets and visitors as irrelevant to Kankurgachhi, and the story quietly demonstrates that contempt for learning is the same contempt they practise for Bonku. When writing, anchor each theme in an episode: the tamarind prank for cruelty, the claimed sighting for injustice, Ang’s courtesy for equality, the final gathering for transformation.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: Answer-writing for this story rewards sequence and evidence. Character questions: give the trait, then the incident that proves it — Bonku’s patience with the children who like him proves his kindness, his silence after the sighting is stolen proves his long habit of yielding. Theme questions: name the theme, define it in your own words, then cite two separated episodes, and close with what the story suggests about the society it depicts. Short-answer questions demand precision about who said or did what — the examinations commonly ask who claimed the sighting, who arranged the prank, where Ang landed — so keep the small facts straight. The technique questions ask about the science-fiction device and the humour; answer both by explaining what the device does for the character, not by retelling the plot. Finally, this page is a guide and not the text: every plot and character detail above follows published summaries and study guides, and your own prescribed edition remains the authority — check any detail you intend to quote in an answer against the pages of the story itself, because the examinations award marks for accuracy about the text, not about a summary of it.

questions.prompt: How long has Bonku Babu been teaching in Kankurgachhi when the story begins?
questions.explanation: Published summaries state that Bonkubihari Dutta has taught geography and Bengali in the village for the last twenty-two years when the story opens.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse the years of service with his age; the text gives his teaching service.

questions.prompt: Who claims credit for the light Bonku had spotted in the sky?
questions.explanation: Bonku shows the light to Nidhi Babu, who takes the credit for having seen it himself at the Saturday gathering — and Bonku keeps quiet.
questions.commonMistake: Sripati Majumdar hosts the gatherings; he does not claim the sighting.

options: In the bamboo grove near the village
On the roof of Bonku’s house
questions.answer: In the bamboo grove near the village
questions.explanation: Published summaries place the landing of the spaceship of Ang, the alien from Craneus, in the bamboo grove on the night Bonku encounters him.
questions.commonMistake: The gathering is where Bonku is mocked; the grove is where the encounter happens.

questions.prompt: According to the men at the gathering, why would no visitor from another planet come to Kankurgachhi?
options: Because aliens are no fools and would choose great cities instead
Because the village has no proper roads
Because the satellite overhead warns them away
questions.answer: Because aliens are no fools and would choose great cities instead
questions.explanation: The regulars assert that sensible creatures would go to Moscow, New York, London or Calcutta — their certainty is exactly what the story then punctures.
questions.commonMistake: The dismissal is social snobbery about the village, not a technical claim.

questions.prompt: The alien who befriends Bonku is named ______ and comes from the planet Craneus.
questions.explanation: Published summaries and workbook notes all give the visitor’s name as Ang, from the planet Craneus.
questions.commonMistake: Spell it Ang; it is a name, not an abbreviation of anything.

questions.prompt: State two indignities Bonku suffers from his students and one from the village gatherings.
questions.answer: From the students: they draw his cartoon on the blackboard and put glue on his chair, and on Kali Puja they lit a rocket right behind him. From the gatherings: they arranged the prank under the tamarind tree that injured his neck and tore his new kurta.
questions.explanation: The question asks for three separate incidents with their sources — school and village — so both sides must be named.
questions.commonMistake: Do not credit the stolen sighting to the students; it happens at the Saturday gathering.

questions.prompt: Why does Bonku endure the teasing instead of protesting?
questions.answer: He believes that if he showed his displeasure he would be dismissed from the post, and that he would not be able to find another one. He stays for the sake of the few children who treat him kindly and enjoy his stories, since teaching them is what makes him feel rewarded.
questions.explanation: The answer has two parts — fear of losing the job and affection for the good students — and both are given in the summaries.
questions.commonMistake: Weakness alone is not the reason; the calculation about employment is the point.

questions.prompt: Describe the encounter between Bonku and Ang, and explain how it changes Bonku.
questions.answer: On the night after the gathering’s mockery, a glowing object descends into the bamboo grove and Ang, a visitor from the planet Craneus, steps out of his spaceship. Published summaries agree that Ang communicates easily with Bonku, demonstrates knowledge and technology far beyond the village’s argument about satellites and rockets, and — the crucial detail — treats Bonku as a companion and an equal rather than as the butt of jokes. The change works on two levels. Inside, Bonku’s accumulated fear unwinds: being valued by a superior being shows him that his low place in the village was assigned by others and not earned by him. Outside, the story shows the result — at the later gathering the same men meet a Bonku who answers back with confidence, and they are left astonished, unable to recognise him. The encounter therefore supplies both the cause and the demonstration of his transformation.
questions.explanation: The description names what Ang does and what that manner does to Bonku, then separates the internal change from the visible one, which is the structure long answers reward.
questions.commonMistake: Do not make the answer about the spaceship’s wonders; the friendship and its effect carry the marks.

questions.prompt: What does the story say about the way communities treat a person they have chosen as their target?
questions.answer: The story shows that such treatment is organised, inherited and continuous. It is organised because the ridicule is distributed — the students take the blackboard and the chair, the gathering takes the nicknames and the pranks, and each member plays a part so that no single person feels responsible. It is inherited because a new batch of students arrives each year and learns the custom without anyone teaching it, which is how the tradition outlasts twenty-two years. It is continuous because even Bonku’s gentleness is used as material: his storytelling, his courtesy and his questions are all turned into comedy for the men at Sripati’s house. The cost is measured in small things — a torn kurta, an aching neck, a sighting given away — and the story’s answer is that the target stops being a target only when he refuses the role, as Bonku does after meeting someone who treats him as an equal.
questions.explanation: The answer analyses the mechanism — distribution, inheritance, continuity — and closes with the story’s remedy, which is interpretation rather than retelling.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the pranks alone retells the plot; the question asks how communities produce the treatment.

questions.prompt: The story needs an alien to rescue Bonku. Discuss whether that is a weakness or a strength of the design, using the story’s events.
questions.answer: It is a strength, and the events prove why. Bonku’s condition — twenty-two years of fear that he would find no other post — cannot be cured by an inner decision alone, because the village has arranged every circumstance to confirm his low status: his sighting is stolen, his question mocked, his patience treated as consent. The story therefore needs an intervention from outside that arrangement, and only something larger than Kankurgachhi can qualify. Ang supplies three things the village withholds: equality, witness and scale. Equality, because he addresses Bonku as a companion; witness, because someone finally sees the ridicule for what it is; scale, because after floating above the village, its opinions are measurably small. Once those are supplied, Bonku’s own courage appears — and the final gathering shows that the courage was his all along, waiting for the lie to be removed. A weakness would have been an alien who solved the problem by force or by humiliating the villagers in return; that would have replaced one injustice with another. Instead the visit changes only Bonku, and the comic astonishment of the men confirms that the transformation is his and not the alien’s. The device, in short, is not a rescue but a mirror.
questions.explanation: The answer takes a position, defends it with the story’s own logic — why inner resolve alone could not work — and distinguishes the used design from a weaker alternative.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely retell the alien episode; the question demands an argument about design.
